title: Tallest Tower Under Height Caps
statement:
A street will get n towers in a row, numbered 1 to n. The planning rules are:

  • Tower 1 must have height 0.
  • Every height is a non-negative integer.
  • Neighbouring towers may differ in height by at most 1.

Some towers also have a cap: caps[j] = [id, limit] means tower id may be at most limit tall. Each id appears at most once, and tower 1 never has a cap.

Return the height of the tallest tower you can build anywhere on the street while obeying every rule.

examples.why: Heights 0 1 1 2 1 0 1 work. Tower 4 can reach 2 between the cap of 1 at tower 3 and the cap of 0 at tower 6; tower 7 only gets back to 1.
No caps: climb by 1 each step from 0 at tower 1 to 4 at tower 5.

The cap of 9 at tower 3 is useless: tower 3 can only reach 2 from tower 1. The low cap at tower 8 pulls the middle down: heights go 0 1 2 3 4 3 2 1 2, peaking at tower 5. Trusting the 9 would wrongly allow more.

hints: Ignore the caps for a moment. With only tower 1 fixed at 0, the best height at tower i is i − 1. How does one cap limit the towers around it?

A cap of L at tower p limits tower i to L + |i − p|. But a cap may itself be unreachable: first tighten every cap using its neighbours on the left and on the right (two passes over the caps sorted by id).

Once caps are tight, between two neighbouring caps (p1, h1) and (p2, h2) the heights rise from both ends and meet at a peak of floor((h1 + h2 + (p2 − p1)) / 2). Also count the stretch after the last cap.

explain.intuition:
Every constraint is a "cone": a cap of L at tower p means tower i can be at most L + |i − p|, because heights change by at most 1 per step. The tallest legal height of tower i is the minimum over all cones, including tower 1's cone 0 + (i − 1). You cannot walk all n towers when n is a billion, but you only need to look between caps.

First make each cap honest. Sort caps by id (with [1, 0] added in front). A left-to-right pass sets h = min(h, prevH + gap), and a right-to-left pass does the same from the other side. Now every cap is actually reachable. Between two neighbouring caps the profile climbs from both ends at slope 1, and the two slopes meet at (h1 + h2 + gap) / 2, rounded down. After the last cap the street just keeps climbing to tower n.
steps: Add [1, 0] to the caps and sort them by id.
Left to right: h[j] = min(h[j], h[j − 1] + (id[j] − id[j − 1])).
Right to left: h[j] = min(h[j], h[j + 1] + (id[j + 1] − id[j])).
For each neighbouring pair, the peak is floor((h1 + h2 + gap) / 2); take the maximum.
Also consider the last cap climbing to the end: h_last + (n − id_last).
pitfalls: Trusting caps as given. A cap of 9 at tower 3 is not reachable; without the left pass the answer overshoots.
Doing only one pass. A low cap far to the right also lowers caps to its left.
Forgetting the open stretch after the last cap, which is often where the tallest tower stands.

complexity.time: O(m log m), m = number of caps

solutions.title: Minimum of all cones, tower by tower
solutions.idea: Each tower's best height is the smallest cap-plus-distance over all caps (tower 1 counts as cap 0). Only works for small n.

solutions.title: Tighten caps both ways, then peak between neighbours
solutions.idea: Sort caps, make each reachable with a left and a right pass, then compute the meeting peak in every gap and the climb after the last cap.

followups: Neighbours may now differ by up to d instead of 1. Where does d enter the formulas?
